correctness.rationale: For an odd prime p, every radix digit sum of 2p that divides 2p must equal 1, 2 or p. Sum 1 forces radix 2p. Sum p implies b-1|p, leaving b=p+1 after excluding binary. Sum 2 allows one nonzero digit 2 (forcing b=p), or two 1 digits: if the trailing place has positive exponent then b=2 and p is a Fermat prime; if the trailing exponent is zero, the base is 2p-1 or a 2-power root of 2p-1, by the odd-exponent factorization. Reverse implications and disjointness are proved. Exceptional primes up to X arise from at most O(log log X) Fermat indices or O(sqrt X) integer squares. The complete proof is in RESULT.md. The separately runnable checker verifies exact sets for 195 primes and a nine-base larger example, without extrapolating from finite data.

originality.rationale: OEIS A080221 introduced the all-base Harshad count in 2003. A100263 lists the five-base family; 2016 entries A271311/A271313 already exhibit square-root, binary and fourth-root examples. These finite examples and the known five/six/seven-base patterns are explicitly credited. The new statement is the exhaustive classification at all odd prime arguments, every higher 2-power root and an O(sqrt X) exceptional-prime theorem. None of the accessible source statements inspected or retrieved implies this complete combined claim. Unlocated stronger previous work remains a real risk.
residual_risks: Searches and available source material cannot rule out an unlocated paper or unpublished proof treating all-base Harshad counts of 2p.
The OEIS six/seven-base patterns overlap several finite cases, so those examples alone are not novel.
A general theorem about radix digit-sum representation could imply this specialization without mentioning Harshad numbers; no such dominating statement was identified in inspected materials.
No independent priority review has occurred.

value.rationale: Even semiprimes are the natural four-divisor test family singled out in A080221/A100263 for unusually small all-base Harshad counts. The theorem replaces empirical five/six/seven-base categories by a complete arithmetic classification for every odd prime, quantitatively identifies the generic five-base regime (at most O(sqrt X) exceptional primes), and exhibits a natural nine-base witness produced by a sixteenth power. The exact count and density are mathematically motivated by the existing sequence questions and require an exhaustive structural proof; no unproved downstream conjecture is used as value.
